messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Keahi was sixty-three when the accident happened, though he still thinks of himself as the man who could fix anything with a steady hand and a calm word. That night he had left a community meeting late, frustrated with a council member who had shouted down a proposal for a new youth center. Keahi had shouted back—something he rarely did—and the anger stayed with him as he drove. He remembers the glare of headlights, the screech of tires, the moment his own car spun across the median. He remembers nothing between that and the taste of blood, the pressure of someone’s hands on his chest, the blur of a police officer’s uniform above him. The rest is missing. He has tried to fill the gaps, but the harder he pushes, the more empty space he finds—like a photograph where only the center is developed. Even now, when his partner at work asks what happened, he opens his mouth and the words are gone, stuck somewhere between his throat and his chest.

After the accident, Keahi returned to his job as a community organizer. He thought he could just pick up where he left off, but the triggers were everywhere. A colleague raised her voice during a planning meeting—not angry, just emphatic—and Keahi felt his hands go cold, his ribs tighten, his mind go blank. He had come to believe that the accident was his fault: if he hadn’t let the council member get under his skin, if he hadn’t driven while still stewing, the crash would not have happened. That self-blame now sat at the center of everything. Because he blamed himself so thoroughly, he began to hear accusation in everyday sounds—a car horn, a door slamming—and see judgment in strangers' glances. When he saw a police cruiser at a stoplight, the uniform triggered a wash of guilt and a sudden, hollow numbness, as though someone had scooped out all his feeling. His body kept responding as if he were still in the car, his heart racing, his palms slick, even though he knew he was safe—and that betrayal made him feel even more dead inside. It was this deadness, he thought, that kept the memory so fragmented. He could not find words for what happened because the numbness drained the color from the story, leaving only a few sharp images that hurt too much to hold.

The gaps themselves fed his guilt. Each missing piece felt like an accusation: *You should remember, you should know, you failed to pay attention then and you fail now.* When a vivid flashback struck—the headlights, the screech—it left him shaking and certain that his own carelessness had caused it all. After each flashback, he found himself jumping at sounds he would have ignored before—a distant siren, the clatter of a garbage truck—as if the memory had rewired his senses to expect danger. And that certainty made him hypervigilant. He started scanning rooms for angry faces, avoiding streets with police stations, steering clear of community meetings he used to lead. The avoidance worked, for a while. But the triggers kept finding him. A passing motorcycle backfire sent him ducking; a neighbor’s raised voice in an argument made him retreat inside. Each time, the numbness deepened, and his memory retreated further, like a turtle pulling into its shell.

The consequences became visible. Keahi stopped volunteering for the late shifts at the community center, then stopped attending the weekly coalition meetings altogether. His co-organizer, a younger woman named Leilani, started covering for him, but she noticed he flinched when she gestured too sharply. He could not explain it to her. When she asked him once if he was okay, he said he was fine, but the word felt like a lie he did not have the energy to maintain.

Finally, after six months of this shrinking, Keahi walked into a therapist’s office. He sat on the edge of the chair and said he needed to get back to the work that mattered. But what he was most afraid of, he admitted quietly, was that he would never remember the whole thing—and that if he did, he would find out he was right to blame himself all along.
